examples.name: Sample — a landscape page in a portrait document
paragraphs: A paper page rendered sideways: the body text, both tables and the Table 3 caption read bottom-to-top. Upright, the two tables are ordinary tables; nothing about them is special except that a reader has to turn the page. The page is cut off after the Kestrel 33B row of the second table, so nothing below it is rendered.

What makes this the useful case is that the rotation is not marked anywhere. There is no landscape flag; the only signal is that the text runs the wrong way. A rendering in page orientation transposes headers and rows and still looks structurally plausible.

Note also the blank corner cells above both stub columns, and the en-dashes standing in for missing benchmark scores — see Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1 and Marks and Symbols in Cells§9.6.6.

examples.name: Sample — a vertical stub header
paragraphs: The leftmost column carries a label running bottom-to-top along the side of the table, spanning every body row, while all the other headers sit horizontally. It labels the whole stub, which is why the typesetter turned it — there was no width for it any other way. The coloured shapes in the second column have no legend on the page, so each is described as drawn.

The rotation is a layout constraint, not a property of the header: the label is rendered upright as a normal header cell spanning the rows it spans. The table's bilingual text and its landscape setting change nothing either.

examples.name: Sample — a landscape reference table on a portrait page
paragraphs: Table C.1. (Cont.): twenty-five chemicals with CAS numbers, formulae and properties, printed sideways. Upright it is an ordinary eleven-column table (No. plus ten property columns); the header cells carry units and subscripts (D_a, cm² s⁻¹), the formulae carry subscripts, and one melting point prints 123.5 decomposes on two lines. The page number C-6, printed beside the title in the table's own orientation, is rendered first as the page's header band.
